cues.text: Welcome to the Diversity identification workshop.
A classification problem is easier when its ranks are written in order.
In the standard school hierarchy, kingdom contains phyla or divisions,
followed
by class, order, family, genus and species.
Moving toward species generally narrows the group.
Two organisms in the same genus share a genus assignment, but they need not be
the same species.
In a binomial name, the first word is the genus and the second is the specific
epithet; the epithet alone is not the full species name.
The genus begins with a capital letter and the epithet with a lower case
letter.
Compare classifications at matching ranks before drawing a relationship.
A single celled organism can be either prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
Bacteria lack a membrane bound nucleus, while protists are eukaryotic in the
conventional school classification.
Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes, so photosynthesis alone does not
make an organism a eukaryotic alga.
Likewise, a visible cell wall does not establish that an organism is a plant.
The classical five kingdom scheme places prokaryotes in Monera, whereas modern
domain classification separates Bacteria and Archaea.
These are different classification frameworks.
Use the framework stated in the question, and combine cellular organisation,
nutrition and other traits rather than treating one familiar feature as a
complete identification.
Both fungi and plants can have cell walls, so a wall alone does not
distinguish
them.
Fungi are absorptive heterotrophs: they obtain nutrients from organic material
rather than fixing carbon by photosynthesis.
Chitin is characteristic of typical fungal walls, while cellulose is a major
component of typical plant walls.
Many fungi grow as hyphae forming a mycelium, but yeasts remind us that fungi
need not all have the same filamentous body form.
A decomposer role is common but not a complete definition, because fungi can
also participate in mutualistic or parasitic relationships.
Use nutrition, cellular traits and body organisation together.
In the standard school comparison, green algae have chlorophyll a and b and
commonly store starch.
Brown algae have fucoxanthin contributing to their colour and characteristic
reserves such as laminarin and mannitol.
Red algae have phycoerythrin as an important accessory pigment and floridean
starch as a characteristic reserve.
These are linked textbook clues, not a rule that every visible colour
photograph is sufficient for identification.
Lighting, pigments and the condition of a specimen can affect appearance.
Also, the broad word algae covers multiple evolutionary lineages in modern
classification.
Read whether the question asks for the school comparison or a modern
phylogenetic grouping before choosing the label.
A typical moss offers a useful bryophyte comparison.
Its conspicuous green plant body is the gametophyte, and the sporophyte
remains
attached and nutritionally dependent to a degree that varies with the group.
Bryophytes lack the true vascular tissues of vascular plants, and their
rhizoids should not be equated with true roots.
In the standard reproductive account, water is needed for the motile sperm to
reach the egg.
Calling bryophytes amphibians of the plant kingdom is a teaching analogy about
this dependence, not a claim that they are animals.
Identify the generation and attachment relationship before naming the stage
shown in a life cycle question.
A typical fern has a dominant diploid sporophyte with vascular tissues and
produces spores rather than seeds.
This contrasts with the dominant gametophyte pattern of bryophytes.
In the usual fern account, a smaller gametophyte participates in sexual
reproduction, and water is still needed for motile sperm to reach the egg.
Some seedless vascular plants, such as Selaginella, are heterosporous,
producing microspores and megaspores.
Heterospory is therefore not, by itself, proof that an organism has seeds.
When an identification key asks whether seeds are present, answer that
question
directly instead of substituting the separate question of whether two spore
types occur.
Gymnosperms and angiosperms both produce seeds, so seed presence alone does
not distinguish them.
In gymnosperms, ovules are not enclosed within an ovary in the angiosperm
sense; the phrase naked seeds describes this contrast and does not mean that
every protective tissue is absent.
Angiosperm ovules occur inside ovaries, and fruits develop from ovaries,
sometimes with contributions from other floral tissues.
Pollen belongs to the male gametophyte generation and is not a seed or embryo.
Use the ovule enclosure and reproductive structure clues when separating these
groups, rather than deciding from leaf shape alone.
Animal identification often combines several independent body plan characters.
Bilateral symmetry has one principal plane producing left and right mirror
halves, while radial organisation permits multiple planes around a main axis
in
the standard comparison.
A true coelom is a body cavity fully lined by mesoderm; a pseudocoelom is not
fully mesoderm lined.
Acoelomate does not mean that every internal space or digestive cavity is
absent.
These terms refer to a specific body cavity comparison.
Developmental stage can also matter: adult echinoderms show radial
organisation
while their larvae are bilateral.
Read the stage and combine the characters before assigning a group from an
identification key.
